notes.front: What is radio propagation, in one sentence?
notes.back: The travel of radio waves from one place to another, and what reflects, bends or absorbs them on the way.
notes.explanation: Propagation decides who can hear you: the same signal may reach a few miles or another continent depending on the path it takes.
notes.example: A 2 m handheld reaches a repeater across town by a direct wave, while an HF sky wave can cross an ocean after the ionosphere bends it back to Earth.
notes.source: US Army, FM 24-18, Tactical Single-Channel Radio Communications Techniques (1987), Glossary (“Propagation”, “Reflection”, “Refraction”) and para 2-3

notes.front: What is line-of-sight propagation?
notes.back: Radio waves travelling in a straight, unobstructed path from the transmitting antenna to the receiving antenna, as light does.
notes.explanation: In the VHF band there is no usable ground wave and only slight bending by the ionosphere, and at UHF the direct wave must be used, so an obstruction in the way blocks the signal.
notes.example: A hill between a handheld and a VHF repeater blocks the signal much as it would block the view.
notes.source: Wikipedia, “Line-of-sight propagation”; US Army, FM 24-18, Tactical Single-Channel Radio Communications Techniques (1987), para 2-3

notes.front: What is refraction of a radio wave?
notes.back: The bending, or change in direction, of a radio wave as it passes into a layer of the atmosphere or the ionosphere.
notes.explanation: Refraction adds a little to line-of-sight range by bending waves over the curve of the Earth, and it bends sky waves back down from the ionosphere.
notes.example: The ionosphere refracts an HF sky wave back down to Earth, far beyond the horizon.
notes.source: US Army, FM 24-18, Tactical Single-Channel Radio Communications Techniques (1987), Glossary (“Refraction”) and para 2-3; NCVEC 2026–2030 Technician Pool, T3C11

notes.front: What is the radio horizon?
notes.back: The farthest point a line-of-sight signal can reach; for VHF and UHF it lies a little beyond the visual horizon.
notes.explanation: The atmosphere refracts VHF and UHF waves slightly, bending them over the visual horizon.
notes.example: Raising your antenna pushes both the visual and the radio horizon farther away.
notes.source: NCVEC 2026–2030 Technician Pool, T3C11; Wikipedia, “Line-of-sight propagation”

notes.front: What is multipath propagation?
notes.back: A signal reaching the receiving antenna by two or more paths, such as direct and reflected from buildings or hills.
notes.explanation: The copies arrive slightly out of step, so they can cancel or reinforce each other, which causes fading.
notes.example: A VHF signal can be strong at one spot and weak a few feet away because the direct and reflected copies add or cancel.
notes.source: Wikipedia, “Multipath propagation”; NCVEC 2026–2030 Technician Pool, T3A01

notes.front: What is “picket fencing”?
notes.back: Rapid flutter on mobile signals due to multipath propagation.
notes.explanation: As a vehicle moves, it passes quickly through spots where the multipath copies add and cancel, so the signal flutters.
notes.example: Like the flicker of sunlight through a fence as you drive past it.
notes.source: NCVEC 2026–2030 Technician Pool, T3A06

notes.front: What is the ionosphere, in one sentence?
notes.back: Earth’s upper atmosphere from about 80 to 600 km, where solar radiation knocks electrons off atoms (ionizes them), leaving a layer of electrons.
notes.explanation: It matters because it reflects and modifies radio waves; its density changes with the Sun, the time of day and the season.
notes.example: The sunlit side of the Earth is much more ionized than the night side, so HF paths change between day and night.
notes.source: NOAA Space Weather Prediction Center, “Ionosphere”
notes.sourceLicence: B · public domain (US government work, 17 USC 105)

notes.front: What is the F region of the ionosphere?
notes.back: The highest main region (about 150–800 km up), with the greatest concentration of free electrons; the main reflector of HF signals.
notes.explanation: The ionosphere has D, E and F layers; the F region, directly above the E region, is the dependable reflector for long-distance HF, and it varies with the sunspot cycle.
notes.example: Near the sunspot peak, the F region can return 10 m and even 6 m signals over long distances.
notes.source: Wikipedia, “F region”; NOAA Space Weather Prediction Center, “Ionosphere”

notes.front: What is skip (skywave) propagation?
notes.back: Radio waves reflected or refracted back to Earth by the ionosphere, so they reach far beyond the horizon.
notes.explanation: Most long-distance HF (3–30 MHz) communication is by skip; it is how amateurs make contacts with distant countries.
notes.example: A 15 m signal from the US returns to Earth in Europe after refracting off the ionosphere.
notes.source: Wikipedia, “Skywave”; US Army, FM 24-18, Tactical Single-Channel Radio Communications Techniques (1987), para 2-3

notes.front: What is the sunspot cycle?
notes.back: The roughly 11-year rise and fall in the number of sunspots, from solar minimum to solar maximum.
notes.explanation: The Sun’s extreme-ultraviolet and X-ray output varies nearly tenfold over the cycle, and the ionosphere’s density changes with it; that is why 10 m and 6 m open for long-distance contacts near the sunspot peak.
notes.example: Solar cycle 24 began in December 2008, peaked in April 2014 and ended in December 2019, when cycle 25 began.
notes.source: NOAA Space Weather Prediction Center, “Sunspots/Solar Cycle” and “Ionosphere”; NCVEC 2026–2030 Technician Pool, T3C10
notes.sourceLicence: B · public domain (US government work, 17 USC 105)

notes.front: What is sporadic E propagation?
notes.back: An uncommon form of propagation off small, dense patches of ionization in the lower E region, about 95–120 km up.
notes.explanation: It can make distant VHF stations heard as clearly as local ones, mainly during the summer months.
notes.example: A distant VHF FM station is briefly heard as clearly as a local one during a summer sporadic E opening.
notes.source: Wikipedia, “Sporadic E propagation” and “Skywave”

notes.front: What is the troposphere?
notes.back: The lowest layer of the atmosphere, where virtually all weather happens; 6–18 km deep, deepest at the equator.
notes.explanation: Its changing temperature, density and pressure affect VHF and UHF signals, which travel through it rather than via the ionosphere.
notes.example: Rain, fog and temperature layers are all tropospheric; the ionosphere lies far above them.
notes.source: US Navy, NEETS Module 10 (NAVEDTRA 14182), Introduction to Wave Propagation, Transmission Lines, and Antennas, chapter 2 (“Troposphere”)

notes.front: What is tropospheric ducting?
notes.back: Propagation along a boundary formed by a temperature inversion in the lower atmosphere, carrying VHF and UHF well beyond the radio horizon.
notes.explanation: Normally air cools with height. In a temperature inversion, warm air lies above cool air, trapping a duct of cool air; VHF and UHF waves that enter it at a low angle travel far beyond normal line of sight.
notes.example: 2 m repeaters about 300 miles away are suddenly heard during a ducting opening.
notes.source: NCVEC 2026–2030 Technician Pool, T3C06, T3C08; US Navy, NEETS Module 10 (NAVEDTRA 14182), Introduction to Wave Propagation, Transmission Lines, and Antennas, chapter 2 (“Temperature Inversion”)

notes.front: What is meteor scatter?
notes.back: Propagation that uses the ionized trails of meteors entering the atmosphere to reflect signals briefly.
notes.explanation: The trails last only moments, so contacts come in short bursts, over paths of up to about 2,250 km.
notes.example: During a meteor shower, two stations 1,000 miles apart exchange signals in bursts lasting seconds.
notes.source: Wikipedia, “Meteor burst communications”

notes.front: What is auroral propagation?
notes.back: VHF signals scattered back from the aurora (auroral backscatter); they arrive distorted, with a characteristic raspy sound.
notes.explanation: The aurora forms 80–500 km up, in ovals round the magnetic poles, where energetic electrons strike the upper atmosphere.
notes.example: During a major geomagnetic storm the auroral ovals expand, and aurora can be seen over most of the United States.
notes.source: NCVEC 2026–2030 Technician Pool, T3C03; NOAA Space Weather Prediction Center, “Aurora”

notes.front: What is knife-edge diffraction?
notes.back: The bending of radio waves around a sharp, well-defined obstacle, such as a mountain ridge or the edge of a building.
notes.explanation: Diffraction lets some signal reach behind obstructions between the transmitting and receiving stations.
notes.example: A VHF signal is still heard in the shadow of a sharp ridge because some of it bends over the edge.
notes.source: Wikipedia, “Diffraction” (knife-edge section); NCVEC 2026–2030 Technician Pool, T3C05

notes.front: What does it mean for antennas to be cross-polarized?
notes.back: One antenna is vertically polarized and the other horizontally, so their electric fields lie at right angles.
notes.explanation: On VHF and UHF a wave keeps its original polarization on the way, so a horizontal transmitting antenna needs a horizontal receiving antenna; a mismatch loses signal strength.
notes.example: A vertical antenna on a car trying to hear a horizontal antenna is cross-polarized.
notes.source: US Army, FM 24-18, Tactical Single-Channel Radio Communications Techniques (1987), para 3-5 (“Polarization”); NCVEC 2026–2030 Technician Pool, T3A04

notes.front: Moving a VHF antenna only a few feet can change signal strength greatly because multipath signals {{c1::cancel or reinforce}} one another.
notes.explanation: The direct and reflected copies add where they arrive in step and cancel where they arrive out of step.
notes.source: NCVEC 2026–2030 Technician Pool, T3A01

notes.front: What effect does multipath propagation have on data transmissions?
notes.back: Error rates are likely to increase.
notes.explanation: Overlapping, out-of-step copies of the signal blur the data, so more bits are received wrongly.
notes.source: NCVEC 2026–2030 Technician Pool, T3A10

notes.front: Irregular fading of ionospheric signals is caused by the {{c1::random combining of signals arriving by different paths}}.
notes.explanation: Multipath happens on HF too: several ionospheric paths combine unpredictably at the receiver.
notes.source: NCVEC 2026–2030 Technician Pool, T3A08

notes.front: How does vegetation affect UHF and microwave signals?
notes.back: It absorbs them, leading to poor reception of weak signals.
notes.explanation: Leaves and trees absorb energy at these short wavelengths, so weak signals suffer most.
notes.source: NCVEC 2026–2030 Technician Pool, T3A02

notes.front: Which weather condition can decrease range at microwave frequencies?
notes.back: Precipitation.
notes.explanation: Rain, snow and other precipitation attenuate microwave signals.
notes.source: NCVEC 2026–2030 Technician Pool, T3A07

notes.front: Fog or rain has {{c1::little effect}} on 10 m and 6 m band signals.
notes.explanation: Weather absorption matters at microwave frequencies, not at these longer wavelengths.
notes.source: NCVEC 2026–2030 Technician Pool, T3A12

notes.front: Long-distance CW and SSB contacts on VHF and UHF normally use {{c1::horizontal}} polarization.
notes.explanation: Stations must match polarization to hear each other well, so weak-signal operators share the horizontal convention.
notes.source: NCVEC 2026–2030 Technician Pool, T3A03

notes.front: Over a line-of-sight VHF or UHF path, what does cross-polarization do?
notes.back: It reduces received signal strength.
notes.explanation: A receiving antenna whose polarization does not match the transmitted wave picks up less of it.
notes.source: NCVEC 2026–2030 Technician Pool, T3A04

notes.front: Because ionospheric signals are elliptically polarized, which antenna polarization can you use for them?
notes.back: Either vertical or horizontal, for transmitting or receiving.
notes.explanation: Because the arriving polarization is elliptical rather than fixed, on HF skip paths the stations' antennas need not match.
notes.source: NCVEC 2026–2030 Technician Pool, T3A09

notes.front: With a directional antenna and buildings blocking the direct path to a distant repeater, what can you try?
notes.back: Find a path that reflects your signal to the repeater.
notes.explanation: Point the antenna at a building or hill that can bounce the signal round the obstruction.
notes.source: NCVEC 2026–2030 Technician Pool, T3A05

notes.front: Which region of the atmosphere can reflect HF radio waves?
notes.back: The ionosphere.
notes.explanation: Its free electrons bend HF waves back to Earth; the stratosphere and troposphere do not.
notes.source: NCVEC 2026–2030 Technician Pool, T3A11

notes.front: Simplex UHF signals are rarely heard beyond the radio horizon because UHF is {{c1::usually not propagated by the ionosphere}}.
notes.explanation: So UHF depends on line of sight and fades out near the radio horizon.
notes.source: NCVEC 2026–2030 Technician Pool, T3C01

notes.front: Compared with VHF and higher, what is characteristic of HF communication?
notes.back: Long-distance ionospheric propagation is far more common on HF.
notes.explanation: The ionosphere bends HF sky waves back to Earth, but in the VHF band it refracts them only slightly and at UHF the direct wave must be used, so skip is mainly an HF matter.
notes.source: NCVEC 2026–2030 Technician Pool, T3C02; US Army, FM 24-18, Tactical Single-Channel Radio Communications Techniques (1987), para 2-3

notes.front: VHF signals received by auroral backscatter are distorted, with a characteristic {{c1::raspy}} sound.
notes.explanation: The aurora forms two ovals roughly centred on the magnetic poles, so auroral backscatter comes from that direction; its hallmark is the rough, raspy sound.
notes.source: NCVEC 2026–2030 Technician Pool, T3C03; NOAA Space Weather Prediction Center, “Aurora”

notes.front: Occasional strong signals on the 10 m, 6 m and 2 m bands from beyond the radio horizon are most commonly due to {{c1::sporadic E}}.
notes.explanation: Sporadic E is irregular, cloud-like patches of unusually high ionization near the E layer; they briefly reflect frequencies that the ionosphere normally lets through.
notes.source: NCVEC 2026–2030 Technician Pool, T3C04; US Navy, NEETS Module 10 (NAVEDTRA 14182), Introduction to Wave Propagation, Transmission Lines, and Antennas, chapter 2 (“Sporadic E”); Wikipedia, “Sporadic E propagation”

notes.front: Which effect may let radio signals travel beyond obstructions between two stations?
notes.back: Knife-edge diffraction.
notes.explanation: The wave bends around a sharp edge, such as a ridge, into the area behind it.
notes.source: NCVEC 2026–2030 Technician Pool, T3C05

notes.front: Tropospheric ducting regularly allows over-the-horizon VHF and UHF contacts to about {{c1::300 miles}}.
notes.explanation: Ducting is the regular over-the-horizon mode for VHF and UHF; it is caused by temperature inversions.
notes.source: NCVEC 2026–2030 Technician Pool, T3C06

notes.front: Tropospheric ducting is caused by {{c1::temperature inversions}} in the atmosphere.
notes.explanation: An inversion is a layer where air gets warmer with height instead of cooler; it forms a boundary that guides signals.
notes.source: NCVEC 2026–2030 Technician Pool, T3C08

notes.front: The band best suited for meteor scatter is {{c1::6 meters}}.
notes.explanation: The frequencies meteor trails can reflect are generally between 30 and 50 MHz, and 6 m (50–54 MHz) is the amateur band closest to that range; contacts come in short bursts as trails form and fade.
notes.source: NCVEC 2026–2030 Technician Pool, T3C07; Wikipedia, “Meteor burst communications”

notes.front: When is the best time for long-distance 10 m propagation via the F region?
notes.back: From dawn to shortly after sunset, during periods of high sunspot activity.
notes.explanation: The F region is ionized by sunlight, so 10 m opens in daylight, and most strongly near the peak of the sunspot cycle.
notes.source: NCVEC 2026–2030 Technician Pool, T3C09

notes.front: Near the peak of the sunspot cycle, the {{c1::6 m and 10 m}} bands may give long-distance contacts via the F region.
notes.explanation: Higher solar activity ionizes the F region enough to return these higher frequencies.
notes.source: NCVEC 2026–2030 Technician Pool, T3C10

notes.front: Why is the radio horizon for VHF and UHF more distant than the visual horizon?
notes.back: The atmosphere refracts radio waves slightly.
notes.explanation: The bending carries signals a little over the curve of the Earth.
notes.source: NCVEC 2026–2030 Technician Pool, T3C11

notes.front: Why do VHF signal strengths sometimes vary greatly when the antenna is moved only a few feet?
notes.back: Multipath propagation cancels or reinforces signals
notes.choices:
A) The signal path encounters different concentrations of water vapor
B) VHF ionospheric propagation is very sensitive to path length
C) Multipath propagation cancels or reinforces signals
D) The Doppler effect causes slight frequency shifts which result in changes in signal strength
notes.choicesExplained: A: water vapour does not change over a few feet. B: VHF is rarely ionospheric. D: Doppler shift needs motion between stations and changes frequency, not strength.
notes.explanation: Multipath copies of the signal cancel or reinforce as the antenna moves.
notes.source: NCVEC 2026–2030 Technician Pool, T3A01

notes.front: How does vegetation affect UHF and microwave signals?
notes.back: Absorbs signals, leading to poor reception of weak signals
notes.choices:
A) Causes knife-edge diffraction, distorting voice peaks
B) Absorbs signals, leading to poor reception of weak signals
C) Amplifies signals, improving reception of weak signals
D) Has no effect
notes.choicesExplained: A: knife-edge diffraction happens at sharp edges, not in foliage. C: vegetation does not amplify signals. D: it does have an effect.
notes.explanation: Trees with heavy foliage absorb radio waves, so a weak UHF or microwave signal that has to pass through them may be lost.
notes.source: NCVEC 2026–2030 Technician Pool, T3A02; US Army, FM 24-18, Tactical Single-Channel Radio Communications Techniques (1987), para 4-1

notes.front: What antenna polarization is normally used for long-distance CW and SSB contacts on the VHF and UHF bands?
notes.back: Horizontal
notes.choices:
A) Right-hand circular
B) Left-hand circular
C) Horizontal
D) Vertical
notes.choicesExplained: A and B: circular polarization is not the weak-signal convention. D: vertical is not the keyed polarization for long-distance CW and SSB.
notes.explanation: Man-made interference is ordinarily vertically polarized, so horizontal antennas pick up less of it; and at VHF and UHF stations must match polarization, so weak-signal operators share one convention: horizontal.
notes.source: NCVEC 2026–2030 Technician Pool, T3A03; US Army, FM 24-18, Tactical Single-Channel Radio Communications Techniques (1987), para 3-5

notes.front: What is the effect of antenna cross-polarization over a line-of-sight VHF or UHF path?
notes.back: Received signal strength is reduced
notes.choices:
A) Modulation sidebands might become inverted
B) Received signal strength is reduced
C) Signals have an echo effect
D) Nothing significant will happen
notes.choicesExplained: A: polarization does not invert sidebands. C: it does not cause echoes. D: the loss is significant.
notes.explanation: Cross-polarized antennas reduce received signal strength on a line-of-sight path.
notes.source: NCVEC 2026–2030 Technician Pool, T3A04

notes.front: When using a directional antenna, how might your station be able to communicate with a distant repeater if buildings or obstructions are blocking the direct line of sight path?
notes.back: Try to find a path that reflects signals to the repeater
notes.choices:
A) Change from vertical to horizontal polarization
B) Try to find a path that reflects signals to the repeater
C) Try the long path
D) Increase the antenna SWR
notes.choicesExplained: A: changing polarization does not get the signal past the buildings. C: the long path does not get a signal round nearby buildings; a reflection off another surface can. D: raising SWR only makes the antenna system worse matched.
notes.explanation: Aim for a reflection path that bounces your signal round the obstruction.
notes.source: NCVEC 2026–2030 Technician Pool, T3A05

notes.front: What is the meaning of the term “picket fencing”?
notes.back: Rapid flutter on mobile signals due to multipath propagation
notes.choices:
A) Alternating transmissions during a net operation
B) Rapid flutter on mobile signals due to multipath propagation
C) A type of ground system used with vertical antennas
D) Interference from cable TV in the form of carriers at fixed intervals across the band
notes.choicesExplained: A: alternating transmissions in a net have another name. C: it is not a ground system. D: it is not cable TV interference.
notes.explanation: A moving vehicle passes quickly through spots where the direct and reflected copies of a signal add and cancel, so the signal flutters.
notes.source: NCVEC 2026–2030 Technician Pool, T3A06, T3A01

notes.front: What weather condition might decrease range at microwave frequencies?
notes.back: Precipitation
notes.choices:
A) High winds
B) Low barometric pressure
C) Precipitation
D) Colder temperatures
notes.choicesExplained: A, B and D: wind, low pressure and cold do not absorb or scatter radio waves; raindrops do.
notes.explanation: Raindrops absorb and scatter radio energy; above 100 MHz scattering is the bigger effect, and above 6 GHz it is greater still, so rain and snow shorten microwave range.
notes.source: NCVEC 2026–2030 Technician Pool, T3A07; US Navy, NEETS Module 10 (NAVEDTRA 14182), Introduction to Wave Propagation, Transmission Lines, and Antennas, chapter 2 (“Rain”)

notes.front: What is a likely cause of irregular fading of signals propagated by the ionosphere?
notes.back: Random combining of signals arriving via different paths
notes.choices:
A) Frequency shift due to Faraday rotation
B) Interference from thunderstorms
C) Intermodulation distortion
D) Random combining of signals arriving via different paths
notes.choicesExplained: A, B and C: fading on ionospheric circuits is mainly a result of multipath propagation, not of Faraday rotation, thunderstorms or intermodulation.
notes.explanation: Signals arrive by several ionospheric paths at once; their copies combine at random, sometimes adding and sometimes cancelling, so the signal fades irregularly.
notes.source: NCVEC 2026–2030 Technician Pool, T3A08; US Navy, NEETS Module 10 (NAVEDTRA 14182), Introduction to Wave Propagation, Transmission Lines, and Antennas, chapter 2 (“Multipath Fading”)

notes.front: Which of the following results from the fact that signals propagated by the ionosphere are elliptically polarized?
notes.back: Either vertically or horizontally polarized antennas may be used for transmission or reception
notes.choices:
A) Digital modes are unusable
B) Either vertically or horizontally polarized antennas may be used for transmission or reception
C) FM voice is unusable
D) Both the transmitting and receiving antennas must be of the same polarization
notes.choicesExplained: A and C: digital modes and FM still work. D: the antennas need not match, because the polarization is not fixed.
notes.explanation: Elliptically polarized ionospheric signals can be used with either vertical or horizontal antennas.
notes.source: NCVEC 2026–2030 Technician Pool, T3A09

notes.front: What effect does multi-path propagation have on data transmissions?
notes.back: Error rates are likely to increase
notes.choices:
A) Transmission rates must be increased by a factor equal to the number of separate paths observed
B) Transmission rates must be decreased by a factor equal to the number of separate paths observed
C) No significant changes will occur if the signals are transmitted using FM
D) Error rates are likely to increase
notes.choicesExplained: A and B: rates are not changed by a factor equal to the number of paths. C: FM does not remove the problem.
notes.explanation: Delayed copies overlap the direct signal, and multipath fading varies with frequency, so the parts of a signal lose their proper phases and amplitudes and data bits are misread.
notes.source: NCVEC 2026–2030 Technician Pool, T3A10; US Navy, NEETS Module 10 (NAVEDTRA 14182), Introduction to Wave Propagation, Transmission Lines, and Antennas, chapter 2 (“Selective Fading”)

notes.front: Which region of the atmosphere can reflect HF radio waves?
notes.back: The ionosphere
notes.choices:
A) The stratosphere
B) The troposphere
C) The ionosphere
D) The electrosphere
notes.choicesExplained: A and B: the stratosphere and troposphere do not reflect HF. D: “electrosphere” is not an atmospheric region used in radio.
notes.explanation: Sky waves travel up to the ionosphere and are refracted (bent downward) back to the Earth.
notes.source: NCVEC 2026–2030 Technician Pool, T3A11; US Army, FM 24-18, Tactical Single-Channel Radio Communications Techniques (1987), para 2-3

notes.front: What effect does fog or rain have on 10-meter and 6-meter band signals?
notes.back: Little effect
notes.choices:
A) Absorption
B) Little effect
C) Deflection
D) Increased range
notes.choicesExplained: A and C: absorption and deflection by weather matter at microwaves, not on 10 m and 6 m. D: weather does not increase range on these bands.
notes.explanation: Fog matters little below 2 GHz, and absorption by weather is a microwave problem; 10 m and 6 m lie far below that.
notes.source: NCVEC 2026–2030 Technician Pool, T3A12, T3A07; US Navy, NEETS Module 10 (NAVEDTRA 14182), Introduction to Wave Propagation, Transmission Lines, and Antennas, chapter 2 (“Fog”)

notes.front: Why are simplex UHF signals rarely heard beyond their radio horizon?
notes.back: UHF signals are usually not propagated by the ionosphere
notes.choices:
A) They are too weak to go very far
B) FCC regulations prohibit them from going more than 50 miles
C) UHF signals are usually not propagated by the ionosphere
D) UHF signals are absorbed by the ionospheric D region
notes.choicesExplained: A: UHF signals are not inherently too weak. B: no FCC rule limits distance to 50 miles. D: the keyed reason is that UHF is usually not propagated by the ionosphere, not D-region absorption.
notes.explanation: UHF signals usually pass through the ionosphere instead of returning, so they depend on the direct wave and stop near the radio horizon.
notes.source: NCVEC 2026–2030 Technician Pool, T3C01; US Army, FM 24-18, Tactical Single-Channel Radio Communications Techniques (1987), para 2-3

notes.front: What is a characteristic of HF communication compared with communications on VHF and higher frequencies?
notes.back: Long-distance ionospheric propagation is far more common on HF
notes.choices:
A) HF antennas are generally smaller
B) HF accommodates wider bandwidth signals
C) Long-distance ionospheric propagation is far more common on HF
D) There is less atmospheric interference (static) on HF
notes.choicesExplained: A: HF antennas are larger, not smaller, because wavelengths are longer. B: HF bands are narrow (the 10 m band is only 1.7 MHz wide), so they cannot carry a 6 MHz TV signal. D: static is worse on HF; the UHF band is noted for its lack of static.
notes.explanation: The ionosphere refracts HF sky waves back to Earth, while in the VHF band it refracts them only slightly and at UHF the direct wave must be used.
notes.source: NCVEC 2026–2030 Technician Pool, T3C02, T8A10; 47 CFR 97.301; US Army, FM 24-18, Tactical Single-Channel Radio Communications Techniques (1987), para 2-3

notes.front: What is one characteristic of VHF signals received via auroral backscatter?
notes.back: They are distorted, with a characteristic raspy sound
notes.choices:
A) They are often received from 10,000 miles or more
B) They are distorted, with a characteristic raspy sound
C) They occur only during winter nighttime hours
D) They are generally strongest when your antenna is aimed west
notes.choicesExplained: A: auroral paths are not 10,000 miles. C: the aurora depends on geomagnetic storms, which spread it toward lower latitudes; the pool ties auroral signals to no season or time of night. D: the aurora lies toward the magnetic pole, north from the US, not west.
notes.explanation: Auroral backscatter reflects signals off the aurora, whose curtains of rays move, twist and sway; the reflected signal comes back distorted and raspy.
notes.source: NCVEC 2026–2030 Technician Pool, T3C03; NOAA Space Weather Prediction Center, “Aurora”

notes.front: Which of the following types of propagation is most commonly associated with occasional strong signals on the 10-, 6-, and 2-meter bands from beyond the radio horizon?
notes.back: Sporadic E
notes.choices:
A) Backscatter
B) Sporadic E
C) D region absorption
D) Gray-line propagation
notes.choicesExplained: A and D: backscatter and gray-line propagation do not bring these sudden strong openings; they come from dense patches of ionization near the E layer. C: absorption weakens signals rather than carrying them.
notes.explanation: Irregular, cloud-like patches of unusually high ionization near the E layer briefly reflect frequencies that the ionosphere normally lets through.
notes.source: NCVEC 2026–2030 Technician Pool, T3C04; US Navy, NEETS Module 10 (NAVEDTRA 14182), Introduction to Wave Propagation, Transmission Lines, and Antennas, chapter 2 (“Sporadic E”)

notes.front: Which of the following effects may allow radio signals to travel beyond obstructions between the transmitting and receiving stations?
notes.back: Knife-edge diffraction
notes.choices:
A) Knife-edge diffraction
B) Faraday rotation
C) Quantum tunneling
D) Doppler shift
notes.choicesExplained: B and C: Faraday rotation and quantum tunnelling do not carry signals past obstacles. D: Doppler shift only changes frequency.
notes.explanation: Knife-edge diffraction bends signals over sharp obstructions.
notes.source: NCVEC 2026–2030 Technician Pool, T3C05

notes.front: What type of propagation is responsible for allowing over-the-horizon VHF and UHF communications to ranges of approximately 300 miles on a regular basis?
notes.back: Tropospheric ducting
notes.choices:
A) Tropospheric ducting
B) D region refraction
C) F2 region refraction
D) Faraday rotation
notes.choicesExplained: B and C: the D and F2 regions are layers of the ionosphere, so refraction there is not the regular 300-mile VHF and UHF mode, which travels in the lower atmosphere. D: Faraday rotation is not a propagation path.
notes.explanation: Tropospheric ducting regularly carries VHF and UHF about 300 miles.
notes.source: NCVEC 2026–2030 Technician Pool, T3C06; NOAA Space Weather Prediction Center, “Ionosphere”

notes.front: What band is best suited for communicating via meteor scatter?
notes.back: 6 meters
notes.choices:
A) 33 centimeters
B) 6 meters
C) 2 meters
D) 70 centimeters
notes.choicesExplained: A, C and D: meteor trails generally reflect 30–50 MHz; 2 m, 70 cm and 33 cm are well above that range.
notes.explanation: Meteor trails generally reflect frequencies between 30 and 50 MHz, and 6 m is the amateur band closest to that range.
notes.source: NCVEC 2026–2030 Technician Pool, T3C07; Wikipedia, “Meteor burst communications”

notes.front: What causes tropospheric ducting?
notes.back: Temperature inversions in the atmosphere
notes.choices:
A) Discharges of lightning during electrical storms
B) Sunspots and solar flares
C) Updrafts from hurricanes and tornadoes
D) Temperature inversions in the atmosphere
notes.choicesExplained: A: lightning does not form ducts. B: sunspots and flares affect the ionosphere, not the troposphere. C: ducting forms in settled, calm high-pressure weather, not in hurricanes and tornadoes.
notes.explanation: A temperature inversion is warm air lying above cool air; the duct of cool air can carry VHF and UHF far beyond normal line of sight.
notes.source: NCVEC 2026–2030 Technician Pool, T3C08; US Navy, NEETS Module 10 (NAVEDTRA 14182), Introduction to Wave Propagation, Transmission Lines, and Antennas, chapter 2 (“Temperature Inversion”)

notes.front: What is generally the best time for long-distance 10-meter band propagation via the F region?
notes.back: From dawn to shortly after sunset during periods of high sunspot activity
notes.choices:
A) From dawn to shortly after sunset during periods of high sunspot activity
B) From shortly after sunset to dawn during periods of high sunspot activity
C) From dawn to shortly after sunset during periods of low sunspot activity
D) From shortly after sunset to dawn during periods of low sunspot activity
notes.choicesExplained: B and D: at night the F region is less ionized. C: low sunspot activity gives poor 10 m propagation.
notes.explanation: The Sun ionizes the F region, so the day side of the Earth is far more ionized than the night side; high sunspot activity raises the ionization enough to return 10 m signals.
notes.source: NCVEC 2026–2030 Technician Pool, T3C09; NOAA Space Weather Prediction Center, “Ionosphere”

notes.front: Which of the following bands may provide long-distance communications via the ionosphere’s F region during the peak of the sunspot cycle?
notes.back: 6 and 10 meters
notes.choices:
A) 6 and 10 meters
B) 23 centimeters
C) 70 centimeters and 1.25 meters
D) All these choices are correct
notes.choicesExplained: B and C: 23 cm, 70 cm and 1.25 m are much higher in frequency; the keyed bands are 6 m and 10 m. D: since B and C are wrong, “all” is wrong.
notes.explanation: The Sun’s extreme-ultraviolet and X-ray output rises nearly tenfold at the peak of the cycle, making the F region dense enough to return 6 m and 10 m; 23 cm, 70 cm and 1.25 m are too high in frequency.
notes.source: NCVEC 2026–2030 Technician Pool, T3C10; NOAA Space Weather Prediction Center, “Ionosphere”

notes.front: Why is the radio horizon for VHF and UHF signals more distant than the visual horizon?
notes.back: The atmosphere refracts radio waves slightly
notes.choices:
A) Radio signals move somewhat faster than the speed of light
B) Radio waves are not blocked by dust particles
C) The atmosphere refracts radio waves slightly
D) Radio waves are blocked by dust particles
notes.choicesExplained: A: radio waves travel at the speed of light, not faster. B and D: dust particles are not what sets the radio horizon.
notes.explanation: The slight bending carries VHF and UHF signals a little way over the curve of the Earth, adding a small distance beyond the visual horizon.
notes.source: NCVEC 2026–2030 Technician Pool, T3C11; US Army, FM 24-18, Tactical Single-Channel Radio Communications Techniques (1987), para 2-3

notes.front: Tropospheric ducting or sporadic E: which happens in the lower atmosphere, and which in the ionosphere?
notes.back: Tropospheric ducting: lower atmosphere, from temperature inversions. Sporadic E: dense patches in the ionosphere's E region.
notes.explanation: Both carry VHF beyond the radio horizon, but ducting is regular (about 300 miles) and sporadic E is occasional.
notes.contrast: Ducting: troposphere, inversions, regular. Sporadic E: E region, occasional.
notes.source: NCVEC 2026–2030 Technician Pool, T3C04, T3C06, T3C08

notes.front: Which reaches farther for VHF and UHF, the visual horizon or the radio horizon, and why?
notes.back: The radio horizon, because the atmosphere refracts radio waves slightly over the curve of the Earth.
notes.explanation: Both depend on antenna height; refraction adds a little extra for radio.
notes.contrast: Visual horizon: straight line. Radio horizon: a little farther, thanks to refraction.
notes.source: NCVEC 2026–2030 Technician Pool, T3C11

notes.front: Rain on a microwave path and rain on a 10 m path: which is weakened?
notes.back: The microwave path; fog or rain has little effect on 10 m and 6 m.
notes.explanation: Weather absorption grows at microwave frequencies; the lower VHF and HF bands barely notice it.
notes.contrast: Microwave: precipitation cuts range. 10 m and 6 m: little effect.
notes.source: NCVEC 2026–2030 Technician Pool, T3A07, T3A12

notes.front: Which ionospheric region is the dependable HF reflector, and which gives only sporadic openings?
notes.back: The F region is the dependable HF reflector; sporadic E comes from patches in the lower E region.
notes.explanation: The F region is highest and densest; sporadic E is uncommon and short-lived.
notes.contrast: F region: dependable HF skip. E region patches: sporadic E.
notes.source: Wikipedia, “F region” and “Sporadic E propagation”
